label: yes
controls_available: WIND THE CLOCK starts the autonomous beat phase.
UP, RIGHT, DOWN, LEFT, and WAIT direction buttons are the simplified mouse action surface; at most one is effective during the gold portion of each beat.
SUBMIT EXPEDITION certifies the recorded result and is administrative rather than outcome-affecting.
autonomous_processes: Before WIND THE CLOCK, the rendered board is static.
After the clock starts, the task pulse progresses continuously; each 1800 ms beat has a 1150 ms action window followed by an off-beat interval in which direction inputs do nothing.

At every beat boundary, the one active crawler automatically moves one Manhattan-reducing tile toward the player using the fixed tie order, or damages the player on contact; the boundary then resets the one-action gate.
After escape, death, or 100 beats, gameplay stops; submission does not change the simulated outcome.
grouped_control_modes: D = simplified direction_buttons across all seeds and attempts: UP, RIGHT, DOWN, LEFT, and WAIT.

clause_i.reason: No observation-free q(I_t) can select a delayed-optimal action for every occurrence in D. The difficulty-1 generator samples the walls, start, exit, and crawler position from the seed, while I_t contains only the prior action/timing history. Identical action histories and beat phases therefore occur with different visible board geometries requiring different directions; the fixed beat schedule alone does not determine the action.

clause_ii.reason: The visible frame renders the complete grid, walls, exit, player, crawler location and health, plus the beat number, moving beat bar, and ACT NOW/LISTEN status. The visible roster and rule identify the crawler as CHASE and state that it chases one tile and acts at the beat boundary. At difficulty 1 the only crawler has no hidden alternating phase, so a policy can read the current frame, predict its one-boundary movement, and plan the delayed-optimal button. The configured 300 ms window has three chronological frames, but its endpoint frame is sufficient; the same visible beat/chase process supplies the prediction.

clause_iii.reason: Use the same crawler process with Delta = 1800 ms, starting shortly inside a gold window so the next delivery is again in the gold window; C_Delta(D) is nonempty because the difficulty-1 state has four hearts and the generated board has a reachable route. A reachable generated state can have player [4,2], crawler [5,4], health 4, and beat 1. If no action is supplied until the next boundary, the crawler visibly advances to [5,3] while success remains possible. In deterministic replay of that board, the shortest successful continuation has Q(H_t, LEFT) = 5 action turns versus Q(H_t, WAIT/no-op) = 6, but after the crawler advance it has Q(H_t^tau, LEFT) = 6 versus Q(H_t^tau, WAIT/no-op) = 6. Thus the LEFT advantage strictly decreases because the crawler relocated, not because of a deadline or later completion alone.

common_visible_process: The common process is the crawler's visible chase at beat boundaries, synchronized with the visible shared-beat bar. The current crawler/player geometry and CHASE rule predict the crawler's next tile, that relocation changes the delayed-optimal direction and can remove a route advantage, and the gold window is where the predicted action must be delivered. The gold-bar deadline is not used as the strict-loss witness.

pre_run.reason: The difficulty-1 generator always creates one live crawler with hp 1 and samples the exit at Manhattan distance at least 3 from the start. After WIND THE CLOCK, act() is the only mechanic operation that moves the player or damages an enemy; the autonomous step only advances the crawler. With no outcome-affecting action after the autonomous phase starts, the player cannot reach the exit or defeat the crawler, and final submission is administrative. Therefore the at-least-half pre-run condition is false; no percentage is asserted.

source_evidence.claim: Difficulty 1 is a 7x7 board with two interior walls, one crawler, one-hit enemies, and four hearts; simplified mode uses direction and wait clicks; the configured observation window is 300 ms with three frames.

The control condition supplies the active difficulty parameters, seeded generation varies board geometry and positions, the board fixes beat_ms=1800/open_ms=1150/max_beats=100, reachability is checked, and the condition is copied into public and truth state.

The browser initializes the visible player/enemy state; act() handles direction or wait actions; step() autonomously moves the crawler or applies contact damage; sync() advances steps as elapsed task time crosses beat boundaries.
The UI visibly renders beat phase, pulse progress, crawler CHASE text, board entities and health, and simplified direction buttons dispatch direction_buttons input.
The authoritative replay uses the same initial state, action, crawler advance, beat timing and simplified input source, and grades the final outcome from the replay rather than trusting the client.

The wiring solver reads the generated public board, plans a route, waits for each beat, and selects the configured direction-button surface for simplified mode; this is implementation evidence of board-conditioned actions.

The shared runtime supplies virtual task time, drains task timers only while running, and runs fixed task-time observation windows; paused/live wall-clock handling is separate from the mechanic's beat state.
The task verifier loads the exported result and the independent clockbeat replay grader, so certification is administrative and does not alter the mechanic outcome.
